prize_parts.citation: for their formal and empirical analysis of how constitutions, electoral rules and state capacity shape fiscal policy and economic development

statement.case_for: B012 founded a field. It gave a formal, testable account of how electoral rules, constitutional design and state capacity determine fiscal policy, redistribution and development, and it is now used across economics and political science. It is distinct from the 2024 recognition. That prize addressed the causal effect of inclusive institutions on long-run prosperity, using colonial settlement as a source of identification, and the commitment-problem theory of institutional persistence. B012 asks a different question: how specific rules and constitutional arrangements generate different policy outcomes and different capacities to tax and provide public goods. The work is three decades old and has been tested, extended and taught for a long time. The attribution is a coherent trio. Persson and Tabellini are the core of the constitutional-rules and political-economics programme, and Besley is closely tied to it through the state-capacity, accountability and development strand, much of it joint with Persson. Since my opening ranking I have not found a better case for moving B012 below first place. I do now think B005 and B011 have cleaner attribution than B012 and are the strongest alternatives.
statement.case_against: Only a minority of members rank B012 at all, and one ranks it last on their list. The cross-country evidence on constitutional and electoral-rule effects is the weakest part of the case. From a measurement perspective it depends on how regimes and electoral systems are coded, and it faces serious reverse-causation concerns. The same question I raised in the 2024 presentation speech, whether the causation runs the other way, applies here. The theory is stronger than the identification, though later work with better designs has narrowed the gap. The area is also diffuse, with many contributors outside the three credited names. My field is adjacent, so I may overrate work that speaks to my own research questions. Finally, the committee may reasonably regard institutions and political economy as recently honoured.

responses.point: B012 forms a natural three-person group with clean core credit, and recent institutions-related recognition covered adjacent but distinct ground. He also notes that structural political-economy predictions are harder to identify cleanly than the headline theory suggests.
responses.response: I agree on both points. The object of study differs from 2024: the 2024 prize addressed whether and why inclusive institutions raise prosperity, while B012 addresses how particular rules map into fiscal and policy outcomes. I would add that his identification caveat is the main weakness, and it is partly a measurement problem. Coding of electoral systems and regimes, and endogeneity of institutional choice, limit what the cross-country regressions can show. I think the case rests on the theoretical framework and on later, better-identified work on state capacity. It should not rest on the early cross-sectional regressions, and a citation should be worded to reflect that.

responses.point: B012 is a founding contribution to political economics, but the 2024 institutions prize may reduce appetite for the area, the field is dispersed across many contributors, and cross-country constitutional comparisons raise identification problems.
responses.response: I accept the identification concern and the dispersion point, and I give them real weight. They are why I do not claim that B012 is clearly the strongest case. I disagree that the 2024 prize should count against B012, though. Recent attention to one theme is not evidence that a different mechanism has been recognised. The question for the committee is whether the contribution is distinct and the credit is separable, and I think both hold. Dispersion does cut against the claim that three names capture the field, and I cannot fully rebut that.

responses.point: Kiyotaki and Moore are the clear originators of the collateral-constraint amplification mechanism. The 2022 prize covered banks and financial crises, which is related but distinct, so a two-name award is clean and the timing is ripe.
responses.response: This is persuasive and has moved me. I ranked B011 sixth mainly out of concern about overlap with 2022, but your account is right. A general-equilibrium mechanism through which asset prices and credit limits propagate shocks is a different contribution from bank runs and the empirical study of banking crises. Attribution is cleaner than in my own first choice, with two names for a single 1997 paper. I now treat B011 as a serious alternative. I still keep B012 first, because I weigh the breadth of the field it opened more heavily than you do. I do not treat the number of members ranking B011 first as evidence of its merit.

responses.point: B012 combines formal theory with empirical identification and ties to long-run development, but the committee must distinguish it from Acemoglu and Robinson's 2024 prize and delimit three names carefully among a broad literature.
responses.response: I agree that delimiting is the central task. The distinction is mechanism versus rules. The 2024 work establishes that institutions matter for prosperity and explains why bad ones persist. B012 explains how electoral and constitutional rules shape fiscal choices and how states acquire the capacity to tax and invest. On the three names, I would not widen the group to others in the literature. The credit is easier to defend if the citation is anchored on the rules-and-capacity programme and does not claim the whole field of political economics.

uncertainties: How much of the cross-country evidence on electoral rules and constitutions survives scrutiny of regime coding and reverse causation, and how much of the case should rest on the theory and on later state-capacity work.
Whether the committee will see B012 as sufficiently distinct from the 2024 institutions prize, or as part of the same theme.
Whether three names capture the field, given contributors outside the credited names, or whether a narrower award would be more defensible.
Whether the 2022 overlap objection to B011 is as weak as Hassler argues. I now think it is, but I have not tested it against the committee's other criteria.
The B005 trade case: how far Redding or the firm-level empirical contributors not credited (for example Bernard and Jensen) should be considered, and how the 2008 trade prize bears on timing.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile with respect to Tabellini, Besley or Persson: none of them appears among my listed collaborators or connections. I disclose that my field (comparative institutions, democratisation, quality of government) is adjacent to B012, so I may overrate it. I hold a chair at Stockholm University, where several IIES-affiliated members are colleagues in a different department. My profile does not tell me whether any candidate has ties to that institution. I also gave the 2024 presentation speech on a neighbouring topic, which does not establish a preference. Per Stromberg's note on Persson's past committee role, I cannot assess it from my profile.
